title: Choosing Transaction Boundaries: Narrowing Them with the Outbox Pattern

blocks.1:
• Load generator: k6 (ramping-vus).
  • Database: MySQL, InnoDB.
  • ORM: Spring Data JPA.
  • Connection pool: HikariCP, maximumPoolSize=10.
  • Metrics:
    • API latency: p50, p95, p99, max.
    • HikariCP active and pending counts.
blocks.5: The reward-earning API, POST /rewards/earn, records a completed order in our database, writes an audit log, and synchronizes with a partner API.
blocks.6: Raising the load to 50 VUs caused response times to spike.
blocks.8: Average latency was roughly 6.2 seconds, with 3,510 requests processed.
blocks.10: Soon after load began, active connections reached the maximum of ten. Pending requests then accumulated, peaking at 35.
blocks.11: That suggested the application was holding connections too long, not simply that the DB was slow.
blocks.13: 2. Why I originally designed it this way
blocks.14: Looking back, putting external HTTP calls inside a transaction seems questionable. At the time, the reasoning felt sensible.
blocks.15:
• If rewards are earned, the audit log and partner synchronization should succeed too.
  • If something fails midway, rolling everything back seems safer.
blocks.16: It looked like one business workflow, so I wrapped it in one transaction.
blocks.17: But a transaction doesn't make every step of a logical workflow atomic. It also determines how long connections and locks remain held.
blocks.20: Two common causes of pool exhaustion are:
blocks.21:
• Slow queries holding connections for a long time.
  • Fast queries inside broad transactions, delaying commit and connection return.
blocks.22: The second looked overwhelmingly likely here. Pending requests accumulated quickly, and requests appeared to stall in one particular part of the flow.
blocks.30:
• The thread waits for the network response.
  • The transaction stays open.
  • The connection and exclusive lock remain held.
blocks.31: External network latency becomes connection-holding time and lock-holding time.
blocks.34: With a pool of ten, if an external call adds an average of 100 ms to each transaction:
blocks.36: It's a simple estimate with important implications.
blocks.37:
• Only ten requests can hold connections; the rest wait.
  • The pending queue grows and p95/p99 climb.
blocks.39: 6. Lock waits tie up more connections
blocks.41:
• Request A holds the exclusive lock while waiting for the partner.
  • Requests B through N wait for the same row's lock.
  • Those requests wait inside transactions, holding their own connections.
blocks.42: When one userId becomes a hot key:
blocks.43:
• A lock queue becomes a connection-holding queue.
  • The entire pool is quickly consumed.
  • Requests for unrelated users are affected too.
blocks.44: Connection scarcity was a visible consequence.
blocks.45: Broad transactions, lock contention, and external I/O combined to exhaust the pool.
blocks.48: Ask which operations actually need to commit together:
blocks.49: OperationAtomic for internal consistency?Benefit of inclusionsummary UPDATE + ledger INSERT✅Highaudit INSERT❌LowPartner API call❌—not atomic with our DBNone
blocks.50: Putting partner synchronization inside a database transaction doesn't make it atomic with that database.
blocks.51:
• External call succeeds, internal DB rolls back: partner credits rewards, internal state doesn't.
  • External call fails, internal DB commits: internal rewards exist, partner state doesn't reflect them.
blocks.52: Consistency with an external system requires idempotency, retries, and asynchronous processing—not just a local transaction.
blocks.55: There are several ways to move the call outside the transaction. The simplest is @Async.
blocks.60:
• Work can be lost when the process restarts.
  • Retries, status tracking, and operational recovery need their own implementation.
blocks.63:
• Database changes and the record of work to perform commit together.
  • Explicit PENDING, DONE, and DEAD_LETTER states support operations.
  • Pending events survive restarts and can be retried.
blocks.65:
• Polling adds delay rather than immediate partner updates.
  • The outbox needs cleanup, indexes, and monitoring.
  • At-least-once delivery requires idempotency.
blocks.66: Losing work was hard to accept, and traceability mattered more. I chose Option B.
blocks.69: The main transaction handles internal consistency only.
blocks.71: A separate scheduler processes the work.
blocks.75: 10.1. Define delay instead of promising immediacy
blocks.76: With a 500 ms polling interval, partner synchronization is no longer immediate.
blocks.77:
• Average polling wait: about 250 ms.
  • Up to about 500 ms of polling wait, plus processing and queueing time.
blocks.78: I chose a bounded polling interval over immediate execution. That is a requirements decision; processing and queueing still add time.
blocks.80: Outbox delivery is generally at least once. Duplicate delivery is possible, so the partner API needs an idempotency key.
blocks.81:
• Use ledgerId as the idempotency key.
  • Repeated requests with the same key must not credit rewards twice.
blocks.82: 10.3. The Outbox is another operational component
blocks.84:
• Monitor and alert on accumulating PENDING events.
  • Clean up DONE rows according to retention policy.
  • Tune polling indexes and batch sizes.
  • Handle DEAD_LETTER events through investigation and manual reprocessing.
blocks.90: Average response time fell sharply, and requests processed in the test increased roughly sixfold.
blocks.92:
• Active connections reached their maximum later and stayed there for less time.
  • Pending counts fell by more than tenfold.
blocks.93: This didn't require query tuning or a broad architectural rewrite.
blocks.94: The improvement came from separating network waiting from transaction resources: connections and locks.
blocks.97:
• A transaction boundary is a resource-holding interval, not just a code block. Business consistency determines what belongs together.
  • External calls inside transactions turn network latency into DB resource occupancy.
  • An Outbox isn't magic. It's a basic mechanism for durable asynchronous work.
  • You pay for it with delayed consistency, operational work, and idempotency design.
